title: Quick Sort
body:
The other divide and conquer sort, and the one that actually gets used. Pick a **pivot**,
partition the [[Array]] so everything smaller sits left of it and everything larger sits
right, then sort the two sides recursively. The pivot is in its final position after the
partition, so there is no merge step: unlike [[Merge Sort]], the work happens on the way
down, not on the way back up.

$O(n \log n)$ average, in place, and with small constants. The catch is the worst case:
a pivot that splits the array 1-to-$(n-1)$ every time gives $O(n^2)$.

```
[7, 2, 9, 4, 1, 5, 8]      pivot = 5
partition ->
[2, 4, 1] 5 [7, 9, 8]      5 is now final
 recurse     recurse
```

## Partitioning

The pivot choice and the partition scheme are the two things that vary between textbooks.
Lomuto's scheme, with the last element as pivot, is the readable one:

```java
int partition(int[] a, int lo, int hi) {
    int pivot = a[hi];
    int i = lo - 1;                       // boundary of the "smaller" region
    for (int j = lo; j < hi; j++) {
        if (a[j] <= pivot) { i++; swap(a, i, j); }
    }
    swap(a, i + 1, hi);                   // pivot into place
    return i + 1;
}

void quickSort(int[] a, int lo, int hi) {
    if (lo >= hi) return;
    int p = partition(a, lo, hi);
    quickSort(a, lo, p - 1);
    quickSort(a, p + 1, hi);              // p itself is done, skip it
}
```

One pass of the loop touches each element once, so a partition is $O(n)$, same as a merge.

## Why the pivot decides everything

| Pivot behaviour | Split | Levels | Total |
|---|---|---|---|
| Median every time | $n/2$ and $n/2$ | $\log n$ | $O(n \log n)$ |
| Typical random data | close enough to even | $O(\log n)$ | $O(n \log n)$ |
| Always the smallest or largest | $0$ and $n-1$ | $n$ | $O(n^2)$ |

The disaster case is not hypothetical. With "first element" or "last element" as the pivot,
**already-sorted input** produces exactly the 1-to-$(n-1)$ split at every level, so the
textbook implementation is quadratic on the most common input in the world. The standard
defences:

- **Median-of-three**: take the median of the first, middle, and last elements.
- **Random pivot**: no fixed input pattern can target it.
- **Fall back to [[Insertion Sort]]** on small subarrays (roughly 10 elements or fewer),
  where its low overhead and $O(n)$ behaviour on nearly-sorted data beat the recursion.

Real library sorts do all three, and some (introsort) count the recursion depth and switch
to heapsort if it gets too deep, which caps the worst case at $O(n \log n)$ outright.

## Trade-offs

| | |
|---|---|
| Time | $O(n \log n)$ average, $O(n^2)$ worst |
| Space | $O(\log n)$ for the recursion stack, no scratch array |
| Stable | no, partitioning swaps distant elements |
| In place | yes |

Against [[Merge Sort]]: quick sort wins on memory and on constants (it does fewer moves and
has better cache behaviour, since it works on contiguous ranges), merge sort wins on the
guarantee and on stability. Java's `Arrays.sort` splits the difference by using a quicksort
variant for primitives, where stability is meaningless, and a merge sort variant for objects,
where it is not.
